title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler is proving that N = 100003 is prime with his idoneal-number criterion. If αβ is idoneal (here 30, and 120 in the shorter method) and N has exactly one representation N = αx² + βy², then N is prime. Starting from 100003 = 10·100² + 3·1², he must show there is no second representation.

Setup from p.17. y must satisfy y ≡ ±1 (mod 10), so y = 1+10z. This gives x² = 10000 − 6z − 30z², and x is even. Splitting by the parity of z gives two equations:
- A: (x/2)² = 2500 − 3a − 30a² (z = 2a)
- B: (x/2)² = 2494 + 27b − 30b² (z = 2b−1)

This page.
- §21, a even: a parity/mod 4 argument forces a = 4c, giving 625 − 3c − 120c² = (x/4)². The subtrahends 120c² + 3c are 117, 123, 474, 486. The remainders 508, 502, 151, 139 are not squares; c = 0 gives the known 25².
- §22, a odd: a mod-8 argument (an odd square is ≡ 1 mod 8) excludes a = 4d+1. With a = 4d−1 he gets 2473 + 228d − 480d². The subtrahends 252, 708, 1464, 2376 leave 2221, 1765, 1009, 97, none of them squares.
- §23, b even: b must be ≡ 2 (mod 4); b = 4e+2 gives 607 − 93e − 120e² = (x/4)². Subtracting 27, 213, 294 leaves 580, 394, 313, none squares.
- §24, b odd: mod 8 forces b = 8g+3, giving 2305 − 1224g − 1920g². Only 696 is subtracted, leaving 1609, not a square; 2305 itself is not a square either.
- Conclusion: the representation is unique, so 100003 is prime, which is correct.

'Brevior methodus' (§§25–27). He writes 100003 = 40·50² + 3·1², with αβ = 120 idoneal. Setting y = 1+20z gives x² = 2500 − 3z − 30z².
- §26, z even: z = 4a gives 625 − 3a − 120a² = x²/4, the same subtrahends as before, so no new square.
- §27, z odd: z = 2b−1 gives 2473 + 114b − 120b². Mod 8 forces b = 4c, giving 2473 + 456c − 1920c²; the subtrahends 1464 and 2376 leave non-squares.
- He concludes primality again, and on the next page infers that larger α, β bring greater savings.

The page thus illustrates the classical idoneal-number primality test with systematic modular (mod 4, mod 8) case pruning.
errors: The 'brevior methodus' (§25) is incomplete. For 100003 − 3y² ≡ 0 (mod 40) one needs y² ≡ 1 (mod 40), i.e. y ≡ ±1 or ±9 (mod 20). Euler's substitution y = 1+20z (with z of either sign) covers only y ≡ ±1 (mod 20). The admissible values y ≡ ±9 (mod 20) (e.g. y = 9, 11) are never examined; for instance y = 9 gives (100003−243)/40 = 2494, an integer.

Because 100003 ≡ 3 (mod 8) forces x even, the forms 10X² + 3y² and 40x² + 3y² correspond one-to-one. The omitted residues y ≡ ±9 (mod 20) are exactly the first method's equation B (§§23–24), whereas §§26–27 reproduce only equation A (§§21–22). The 'shorter method' is therefore just the first method with half the cases silently dropped, not a genuine saving.
The conclusion is still correct only because §§23–24 had already excluded case B. Euler's ensuing claim (p.20) that larger α, β yield more 'lucrum' is not supported by this example.

Minor: in §22 the condition a = 4d−1 could be sharpened by mod 8 to a ≡ 7 (mod 8), i.e. d even (d = ±1 give remainders ≡ 5 mod 8); §27 implicitly uses this. Euler also omits listing the trivial checks d = 0 and e = 0 (2473 and 607 are not squares). The work is harmless but redundant.

ideas.what: Primality proof via uniqueness of representation by a form αx²+βy² with αβ idoneal ('numerus idoneus')
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (later Gauss's genus theory explains it)
ideas.where_published: E498, E708, E715, E719, E725 and related idoneal-number papers

ideas.what: Reducing the search for a second representation to checking whether K − (quadratic in t) is a square, pruning cases via residues mod 4 and mod 8 (odd squares ≡ 1 mod 8)
ideas.modern_name: Sieving solutions of a quadratic Diophantine equation with congruence conditions (exclusion method)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; later systematized by Gauss's 'method of exclusion' (Disquisitiones §§319ff.)
ideas.where_published: E715/E719 and Euler's other factoring papers

ideas.what: Choosing a representation with larger coefficients (40·50²+3) to shorten the search
ideas.modern_name: Using a larger idoneal discriminant to reduce search range

missed.claim: Euler's 'shorter method' for N = 100003 (α = 40, β = 3) silently omits the residue classes y ≡ ±9 (mod 20). It amounts to only half (case A) of the first method, so the advertised saving rests on a logical gap. The primality conclusion survives only because case B had been checked earlier. I am unsure whether the Opera omnia editors flag this.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A small correction to the historical record of Euler's idoneal-number primality method. It also shows that its efficiency claims must account for all square roots of 1 modulo 4αβ, not just ±1.

deep.surprise_reason: The method and result (100003 prime via idoneal number 30/120) are well known. The only non-routine finding is a gap in the 'brevior methodus': missed residue classes, masked by the earlier full computation. It is a minor, possibly already-noted slip.
transcription_corrections: §25: the reduced equation is 2500 − 3z − 30zz = xx, not 250000 − 3z − 30zz.
§26: 'defumti' should read 'desumti'; the right-hand side xx/4 is correct.
